
# Biological Pattern Discovery with R

## 6.2.4 How to discover DEGs using the limma package

To gather DEG information together, limma provides a function called topTreat and its use can generate a spreadsheet shown in Table 6.3.

```r
top.model=topTreat(treat(sam.model),
number=nrow(X))
head(top.model)
```

Figure 6.10. The heatmap of 20 DEGs for the prostate cancer data. 'P' stands for the primary tumour and 'M' stands for the metastasis tumour. The DEGs were detected using both the biological significance and the statistical significance.

To show how DEGs contribute to the discrimination power between two classes of tumours of the prostate cancer data, the heatmap for top 20 DEGs was generated and based on both the biological significance and the statistical significance. It can be seen that two classes of tumours were separated using these top 20 DEGs. The primary tumours (denoted by P) were clustered into the right cluster and the metastasis tumours (denoted by M) were clustered into the left cluster.

## 6.3 DEG discovery for RNA-seq sequencing count data

Along with the significant cost reduction of the sequencing technology, analysing gene expression pattern or detecting differentially expressed genes based on sequencing count data has been more and more popular in biological/medical research. The sequencing count data are normally generated using the next-generation sequencer such as the so-called Illumina machine [Behajati and Tarpey, 2013; Forde and O’Tool, 2013; van Dijk, et al., 2014]. A next-generation sequencer generates short sequences, which are normally 100 base pairs long or shorter. Such a short sequence is called a sequencing read. One of the major applications of the sequencing count data is the transcriptome data for gene differential expression pattern discovery [Crowgey, et al., 2020; Goswami and Harada, 2020]. Therefore, the majority of the sequencing count data used for discovering differentially expressed genes is called the RNA-seq count data.

It must be noted that an individual sequencing read has no biological meaning. The biological meaning of sequencing reads can be investigated only when they have been aligned or mapped to a reference genome. There are several packages for mapping or align sequencing reads to a selected reference genome, such as BWA [Li and Darwin, 2009] and Bowtie [Langmead, et al., 2009]. An active gene may attract a greater amount of sequencing reads while an inactive gene may attract little or no sequencing reads. Only after sequencing reads have been mapped (aligned) to a reference genome, it is possible to assess whether a gene is more active and less active than other genes depending on the number of sequencing reads which hit the gene. The direct outcome of the mapping from sequencing reads to a reference genome is a sequencing count matrix across genes and replicates. Only after such a matrix has been generated, discovering DEGs based on sequencing count data can then follow.

In a sequencing count matrix, genes are arranged in rows and replicates are arranged in columns. Each entry of such a matrix stands for the number of sequencing reads hitting a gene of a replicate, i.e., the sequencing count in one replicate for one gene. Table 6.4 shows such a count matrix used to examine how genes contribute to the airway smooth muscle cytokine function [Himes, et al., 2014], where there were two experimental conditions and each condition had four replicates. The objective of analysing such a sequencing count matrix was to find out which subset of genes are differentially expressed.

Table 6.4. A count after the sequencing reads have been mapped to a reference genome. Each count represents the times the sequencing reads hit a gene. Gene IDs were shortened by removing prefixes ENSG000000 and sample IDs were shortened by removing SRR10395.

| Gene | 08 | 09 | 12 | 13 | 16 | 17 | 20 | 21 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 003 | 723 | 486 | 904 | 445 | 1170 | 1097 | 806 | 604 |
| 005 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | |
| 419 | 467 | 523 | 616 | 371 | 582 | 781 | 417 | 509 |
| 457 | 347 | 258 | 364 | 237 | 318 | 447 | 330 | 324 |

The sequencing count data are different from microarray data as count data are non-negative integers. Therefore, limma may not be useful. The negative binomial distribution has been employed for identifying DEGs for the sequencing count data [Robinson, et al., 2009; Anders and Huber, 2010].

### 6.3.1 Discover DEGs for sequencing count data using DESeq2

DESeq2 is a package developed for gene differential expression discovery based on a sequencing count set [Love, et al., 2014]. The first thing to do is to generate a design matrix. Table 6.5 shows a design matrix for the data in Table 6.4. In this matrix, the column labelled by id is for names of replicate. The column labelled by dex is for classifying two experimental conditions, namely control and treated. By comparing the column id and the column dex, all samples in the count matrix were classified. Other columns contained information regarding an experiment, which were commonly irrelevant to DEG discovery, but for further analysis.

Table 6.5. A design matrix for the data of Table 6.4.

| id | celltype | geo id |
|---|---|---|
| SRR1039508 | control | N61311 | GSM127562 |
| SRR1039509 | treated | N61311 | GSM127563 |
| SRR1039512 | control | N052611 | GSM127566 |
| SRR1039513 | treated | N052611 | GSM127567 |
| SRR1039516 | control | N080611 | GSM127570 |
| SRR1039517 | treated | N080611 | GSM127571 |
| SRR1039520 | control | N060111 | GSM127574 |
| SRR1039521 | treated | N060111 | GSM127575 |

Suppose a count matrix shown in Table 6.4 was saved in X and a design matrix shown in Z. A working data was generated by DESeqDataSetFromMatrix of DESeqs. The parameter tidy was switched on because the first column of the count matrix data was the gene names.

```r
Q=DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData=X, colData=Z, design=~class, tidy=TRUE)
```

The data structure of Q is a DESeqDataSet data structure. The sequencing count matrix had 38,694 genes and eight samples. The assay type was the sequencing counts. The prefix of gene IDs is ENSG000000000. The prefix of sample names is SRR10395. The sample classification ID was dex. Q is an S4 object in R and its entries can be viewed using `slotNames`. Based on this working data Q, a DESeq model can be constructed using the following code,

```r
model=DESeq(Q)
```

In order to obtain statistics as the p values, the results must be based on a DESeq model. This generates a table of results shown in Table 6.6.

```r
res.table=results(model)
```

Table 6.6. The head of results table (res.table) for the airway data. 'ID' is a short name with ENSG00000000. 'B' stands for baseMean, 'F' stands for log2FoldChange.
